chatbot-in.title: The question
chatbot-in.body: A chatbot takes one message in. Everything it knows about the task has to be in that message or in its training.

chatbot-model.title: One model call
chatbot-model.body: The model reads the question and writes an answer in a single call. It can't look anything up or take an action.

chatbot-out.title: The answer
chatbot-out.body: Fast and cheap. Good when the answer is already in the model's head, poor when the task needs steps or fresh data.

workflow-in.title: Workflow input
workflow-in.body: A workflow starts the same way every time. The developer has already decided every step that follows.

workflow-s1.title: Fixed step 1
workflow-s1.body: Each step is written by the developer: for example, look up the booking. The model may help inside a step, but it doesn't choose the order.

workflow-s2.title: Fixed step 2
workflow-s2.body: Steps always run in this order. That makes workflows predictable, cheap and easy to test.

workflow-s3.title: Fixed step 3
workflow-s3.body: If the task needs a step nobody wrote, the workflow can't adapt. That's why it does poorly on open-ended tasks.

workflow-out.title: Workflow output
workflow-out.body: Best for known, repeatable processes, where the cost of a surprise is high.

agent-in.title: The goal
agent-in.body: An agent gets a goal, not a list of steps. It works out the steps itself.

agent-model.title: The model decides
agent-model.body: Each time round, the model looks at what it has so far and picks the next action. This choice is what makes it an agent.

agent-search.title: A search tool
agent-search.body: The agent asks the application to run a search. The application runs it and returns the results to the model.

agent-db.title: A booking tool
agent-db.body: Another tool the agent can call. Every call adds time, tokens and a chance of error.

agent-out.title: The result
agent-out.body: Agents handle open-ended work well, but cost more and are less predictable than a workflow.

multi-agent-in.title: The goal
multi-agent-in.body: A multi-agent system splits a big goal between several agents.

multi-agent-lead.title: Lead agent
multi-agent-lead.body: The lead plans the work, hands out subtasks and merges the results. Every handoff can lose detail.

multi-agent-w1.title: Worker agent A
multi-agent-w1.body: Works on its own subtask with its own context, in parallel with the other worker.

multi-agent-w2.title: Worker agent B
multi-agent-w2.body: Parallel work finishes sooner, but each agent reads and writes its own tokens, so the total cost adds up fast.

multi-agent-out.title: Merged result
multi-agent-out.body: Worth it for independent, parallel work. For tightly linked steps, one agent is usually better.

assess.title: Assess
assess.body: The agent reads the goal and everything that has happened so far. Its context grows each time round, so each step costs more.

decide.title: Decide
decide.body: The model chooses the next action, usually a tool call. In a workflow, the developer makes this choice instead.

act.title: Act through a tool
act.body: The application runs the tool the model asked for. Tools fail sometimes; set Tool failure rate to see what that does to the loop.

check.title: Check the result
check.body: The agent looks at what the tool returned and asks whether the goal is met. If not, it goes round again.

budget.title: Token budget
budget.body: Every pass spends tokens. Without a limit, a loop that keeps failing spends until the budget runs out.

limit.title: The brake
limit.body: A step limit stops the loop early and hands the task to a person, at a fraction of the cost of running away.

tank.title: A stock
tank.body: A stock is something that builds up or drains over time. Here it's the context window, measured in tokens.

inflow.title: Inflow
inflow.body: Each turn adds conversation history and tool results. More in than out means the stock keeps rising.

outflow.title: Outflow
outflow.body: Summarising old turns and removing stale tool results drains the stock. Match it to the inflow and the level holds steady.

limit.title: The hard limit
limit.body: The context window has a fixed maximum. Past it, old content has to be cut, and answers get much worse.

sixty.title: Quality starts to drop
sixty.body: Long before the limit, a fuller window means more for the model to attend to, so quality starts to slip.

clients.title: Clients
clients.body: Each block is a client sending one request per second. Together they set the steady demand.

provider.title: The model provider
provider.body: It can serve a fixed number of requests per second. When overloaded, it wastes work on requests that time out, so it serves even fewer.

storm.title: Reinforcing loop
storm.body: Failed requests are retried straight away, which adds load, which causes more failures. This is a retry storm.

brake.title: Balancing loop
brake.body: Backoff with jitter spreads retries out, and a retry budget caps them. Together they keep load near capacity.

capacity.title: Capacity line
capacity.body: Bars above this line mean more requests arrived than the provider could serve that second.

token.title: A token
token.body: Text is split into tokens: whole words, or pieces of longer words. Click a token to see what it pays attention to.

layer.title: A layer
layer.body: Each layer mixes information between tokens and refines what each one means in context. Real models stack dozens.

attention.title: Attention
attention.body: The arcs show which earlier tokens this token draws on most. Thicker arcs mean more attention.

probability.title: Next-token probability
probability.body: The model gives every possible next token a probability. Temperature reshapes these bars before one is picked.

window.title: The context window
window.body: Only tokens inside this frame can affect the prediction. Tokens that fall outside it are invisible to the model.

position.title: Positional encoding
position.body: Attention on its own can't tell word order. A position signal is added to each token's vector so the model knows which token came first.

residual.title: The residual stream
residual.body: Each token's vector travels up this line through every block. Each sub-layer reads it and adds its result back, so information builds up layer by layer.

attention-layer.title: Self-attention
attention-layer.body: Every token looks back at the tokens before it and pulls in information from the ones that matter. The arcs show where the focused token is looking.

head.title: An attention head
head.body: Each block has several heads that look for different things at once: related meaning, the previous token, the start of the text, recent words. Real models have dozens per block.

unembed.title: Unembedding and softmax
unembed.body: The last token's final vector is compared with every word in the vocabulary to give a score, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.

mlp.title: Feed-forward layer
mlp.body: After attention, each token is processed on its own: its vector expands into many more numbers, passes through a non-linearity, and contracts back. This is where most of a model's stored knowledge lives.

input.title: Input neuron
input.body: Holds one feature of the message, from 0 to 1. Change it with the sliders and watch the signal flow forward.

hidden.title: Hidden neuron
hidden.body: Adds up its inputs, each multiplied by a weight, plus a bias, then squashes the total. Click it to change its bias.

output.title: Output
output.body: The two outputs become probabilities that add up to 100%. The bigger sphere is the network's choice.

weight.title: A weight
weight.body: A weight multiplies the signal that travels along this connection. Mint is positive, pink is negative, and thickness shows the size. Use the Weight slider to change it.

surface.title: The error surface
surface.body: Each point is a pair of weights; height is the error with those weights. You clicked here, so the ball now starts at this point.

ball.title: Current weights
ball.body: Training only knows the height and slope right here. Each step moves the ball a little way downhill.

trail.title: An earlier step
trail.body: Each dot is where the weights were after one training step. Watch the gaps shrink as the slope flattens.

minimum.title: The lowest error
minimum.body: The best weights on this surface. Training aims here but may stop in a shallower dip on the way.

app.title: Your app
app.body: Builds the request: the model name, system prompt, the whole conversation so far and max_tokens. The model remembers nothing, so history is sent every time.

internet.title: The internet
internet.body: The request travels as JSON over HTTPS. This hop adds tens of milliseconds each way.

gateway.title: API gateway
gateway.body: Checks your API key and your rate limit before anything reaches a model. A wrong key gives 401; too many requests give 429.

tokenizer.title: Tokenizer
tokenizer.body: Splits your input into tokens. Input tokens are what you pay for on the way in.

model.title: Model on GPUs
model.body: Reads all input tokens at once, then writes the answer one token at a time. Writing is the slow part.

gpu.title: GPUs
gpu.body: The model runs on accelerators that do the huge matrix multiplications for every token.

request-path.title: The request path
request-path.body: Your request's route to the model: app, internet, gateway, tokenizer, model.

return-path.title: The response path
return-path.body: With streaming, each token comes back as soon as it's made, so the first words appear early. Without it, everything waits for the last token.

requests.title: Requests
requests.body: Fifty requests that each need a JSON answer in a fixed shape.

model.title: The model
model.body: Usually returns valid JSON, but not always. Model reliability sets how often.

validator.title: Validator
validator.body: Checks every output against the schema before anything uses it. Without it, broken output goes straight to users.

users.title: Users
users.body: Green blocks are good answers; red ones are broken output that reached a user.

retry.title: Retry once, with the error
retry.body: Send the request again with the validation error included. This fixes most failures.

fallback.title: Fallback
fallback.body: A simpler, safe path, such as a fixed reply or a smaller task, used when the retry also fails.

person.title: A person
person.body: The last resort. Reliable, but it costs the most and takes the longest.

conveyor.title: The flow
conveyor.body: Every output passes this way. The contract decides what happens at each point.

requests.title: Requests
requests.body: Bigger cubes are harder tasks. Most real traffic is easy.

router.title: Router
router.body: Sends each request to a model based on how hard it looks. The threshold sets where the split is.

small.title: Small model
small.body: Fast and cheap, and accurate on easy tasks. It struggles on hard ones.

large.title: Large model
large.body: Slower and about 15 times the cost here, but accurate on hard tasks.

answers.title: Answers
answers.body: Green answers are right, red are wrong. Compare cost, speed and accuracy across routing choices.

role.title: Role
role.body: Tells the model who it is and who it serves. Click the slab to switch it on or off.

goal.title: Goal
goal.body: What a good outcome looks like. Keeps the model on task.

rules.title: Rules
rules.body: What the model must and must not do, such as quoting policy only from the documents.

reasons.title: Reasons for rules
reasons.body: Why each rule exists. Models apply rules more accurately in edge cases when they know the reason.

format.title: Output format
format.body: The exact shape of the reply, such as a JSON schema. Your code can then check it.

examples.title: Examples
examples.body: Two or three varied examples of ideal replies. They teach format and tone better than description.

missingInfo.title: Missing-info rule
missingInfo.body: What to do when information is missing: ask for it, rather than guess.

contradiction.title: A contradictory rule
contradiction.body: A rule that clashes with another. Adding rules for every failure often creates these, and they break tests that used to pass.

window.title: The context window
window.body: Everything the model sees in one call. Its length here is the full token limit.

limit.title: Window limit
limit.body: Anything past this line doesn't fit. Something has to be cut, and quality drops sharply.

system.title: System instructions
system.body: The standing prompt: role, rules and format. Stable, so it's a good candidate for caching.

tools.title: Tool definitions
tools.body: Every tool's name, description and schema. Many tools take a lot of room.

retrieved.title: Retrieved documents
retrieved.body: Loading all documents upfront fills the window with mostly irrelevant text. Loading only what the question needs keeps it small.

history.title: Conversation history
history.body: Grows every turn. Summarising old turns keeps what matters at a fraction of the size.

tool-results.title: Tool results
tool-results.body: Old tool results pile up fast and are rarely needed again. Dropping them frees a lot of space.

notes.title: Progress notes
notes.body: Notes stored outside the window and read back in, so long tasks keep their place without carrying everything.

overflow.title: Overflow
overflow.body: This part doesn't fit in the window. In a real system it would be cut or the call would fail.

cached.title: Cached prefix
cached.body: This part is the same on every call, so the provider can reuse it at a fraction of the price. The model still sees it.

meter.title: Answer quality
meter.body: Falls as irrelevant material crowds the window, and falls hard past the limit. A teaching approximation.

query.title: Your query as a vector
query.body: The query is turned into a vector with the same embedding model, so it lands near chunks with similar meaning.

link.title: A retrieved chunk
link.body: A line joins the query to each of the top-k results. Only these few chunks go into the model's context window.
